models_evaluated: synthetic reinforcement-learning-style AI dosing recommender (simulated, not a real system)

links.outcome: Whether physicians detected and rejected unsafe AI dosing recommendations
links.effect: Unsafe recommendations stopped 83±4% vs safe 29±4% (p<0.0001); 92% when including senior-help requests; some unsafe advice still accepted.
links.quote: In total, unsafe AI recommendations were stopped more often than safe AI recommendations (83 ± 4%, 95% CI: 0.75–0.91 vs. 29 ± 4%, 95% CI: 0.21–0.37, p < 0.0001).

links.outcome: Human-AI team behavior in a high-fidelity simulation, including AI influence on physician decisions
links.effect: Physicians changed prescriptions in 46% (105/228) of trials after seeing AI advice; unsafe recommendations mostly rejected, showing human-AI behavior needs assessment beyond standalone AI.
links.quote: Physicians changed their prescription (dose of fluids and/or vasopressors) in 46 ± 3% (105/228), 95% CI: 0.40–0.52, of trials after seeing what the AI suggested.

links.outcome: Clinician performance with AI in simulated intended workflow, including effect on decisions
links.effect: AI advice altered treatment decisions; 92% of unsafe recommendations stopped or escalated versus 29% of safe ones stopped, which standalone metrics would not reveal.
links.quote: The proportion stopping unsafe AI recommendations rose to 92 ± 3%, 95% CI: 0.86–0.98 (p = 0.0823) when including physicians who asked for a senior opinion, which would most likely lead to the unsafe AI recommendation being rejected (see Fig 3a ).

links.outcome: Whether AI explanations drew more visual attention when recommendations were unsafe
links.effect: Fixations on AI explanation ROI not significantly different between safe and unsafe scenarios, questioning explanations as a mitigation.
links.quote: Finally, the number of gaze fixations on the AI explanation ROI was not significantly different between safe and unsafe scenarios.

links.outcome: Whether physicians verified unsafe AI outputs against clinical data before acting
links.effect: No increased fixations on the chart or monitor after an unsafe AI reveal; clinicians did not look back to debug the AI, though most unsafe recommendations were rejected.
links.quote: Nor did physicians devote significantly more attention to looking back at the ‘traditional’ (non-AI based) clinical data after seeing an unsafe AI recommendation to understand why the recommendation might be unsafe (i.e., there was no outward evidence of a desire to ‘debug’ the unsafe AI recommendation).

links.outcome: Senior/second opinion requests after seeing unsafe versus safe AI recommendations
links.effect: Second-opinion requests rose from 40% to 57% after unsafe AI (p=0.016); unsafe vs safe 57% vs 36% (p=0.0051); juniors asked more often than seniors (70% vs 28%).
links.quote: Seeing an unsafe rather than a safe AI recommendation triggered more senior/second opinion requests (57 ± 6%, 95% CI: 0.45–0.69 vs. 36 ± 4%, 95% CI: 0.28–0.44, p = 0.0051).

links.outcome: Human-AI interaction safety not captured by retrospective validation
links.effect: Told AI was validated retrospectively but not prospectively; unsafe recommendations were still sometimes accepted, and the authors note retrospective validation is insufficient.
links.quote: Still, the necessity of prospective and higher fidelity evaluations involving clinical end users is clear from recent examples in other fields [ 13 ].

links.outcome: Effect of peer (nurse) persuasion on physician decisions about unsafe AI recommendations
links.effect: Nurse's scripted challenge did not change decision in 95±4% of cases; two junior participants were persuaded to accept an unsafe recommendation. Briefing/education was hypothesized, not tested.
links.quote: In 95 ± 4% (95% CI: 0.87–1.03) of cases (), the verbal input challenge from the bedside nurse did not change the decision of the physician to accept or reject the automated application of the AI recommendation.

models_evaluated: synthetic/fictitious ICU sepsis dosing AI recommender system

links.effect: Unsafe AI shifted fluids by 40 ml/h and vasopressors by 0.08 mcg/kg/min; safe AI shifted 80 ml/h and 0.01 mcg/kg/min.
links.quote: Both safe and unsafe AI recommendations influenced human decisions to different extents: fluid doses shifted on average by 80 ml/h (and vasopressor doses by 0.01 mcg/kg/min) after a safe AI recommendation compared to 40 ml/h (and 0.08 mcg/kg/min) after an unsafe AI recommendation.

links.outcome: checking clinical data after unsafe AI
links.effect: Clinical information did not receive more attention after unsafe versus safe AI reveal; no numeric effect reported.
links.quote: Similarly, clinical information (patient monitor, patient chart) did not receive more attention after an unsafe versus safe AI reveal suggesting that the physicians did not look back to these sources of information to investigate why the AI suggestion might be unsafe.

links.effect: Unsafe recommendations stopped 83 ± 4% versus safe 29 ± 4%; stopped/escalated unsafe recommendations rose to 92 ± 3%.
links.quote: In total, unsafe AI recommendations were stopped more often than safe AI recommendations (83 ± 4%, 95% CI: 0.75–0.91 vs. 29 ± 4%, 95% CI: 0.21–0.37, p < 0.0001).

links.outcome: Physician rejection of unsafe versus safe AI treatment recommendations
links.effect: Unsafe AI recommendations were stopped more often than safe ones (83 ± 4%, 95% CI: 0.75–0.91 vs 29 ± 4%, 95% CI: 0.21–0.37, p < 0.0001), rising to 92 ± 3% with senior consultation.
links.quote: In total, unsafe AI recommendations were stopped more often than safe AI recommendations (83 ± 4%, 95% CI: 0.75–0.91 vs. 29 ± 4%, 95% CI: 0.21–0.37, p < 0.0001).
